paragraphs.text: I. A Panegyric Delivered to the Most Clement King Theodoric.

Venerable prince, let a man's calling forbid him to write your praises, and regard for his vocation keep him from proclaiming you, if some office has kept him from your protection. But let the whole people, bound to you by your benefits, pour back their words to you; in an unequal exchange, let them repay with praise what they gained by your sweat. Liberty, indebted to your arms, has learned to announce its joy in proclamations, which is all it can do. It is for you, illustrious one, to set a value on a devotion that, as you understand, cannot go beyond the powers of your subjects. Your sacred stewardship will judge what to ask of your servants, for you know that all their strength serves you. May your majesty deign to accept this literary offering at its own altars, for if the splendour of deeds is not to grow old, the skills of the tongue must be called in. Let a chain of narrators hold fast what you have done, so that time does not claim it for itself; you will grant peace to those studies through which eternity will come to you. The heavenly steward of mysteries asks nothing more of human minds than that they understand from what author their wisdom comes. Among those nearest to God, to have recognized the giver is to have repaid the gift. What comes down from above may be priced only at the wage of hymns, and the Maker of the world is invited to greater gifts by measured speech. Tell me, then: should I not flatter the Maker with his own tongue in place of a reward? Add to this that a prince's praise ought to flow from the sanctuary of a pure heart. To honour your divinity, which a good conscience must affirm, polish of the tongue is not enough. In divine worship a serene mind performs the sacrifice even with its mouth at rest; a man fortified by the brightness of his deeds serves in heavenly worship even when he is silent. Therefore my title too, which was thought to stand in the way, invites me. Would that my purer profession might agree with what lies hidden within me, and that the splendour of my heart might not be at odds with my body.

Hail now, greatest of kings, under whose rule the vigour of free birth has found its savour again. Hail, safety of the commonwealth! It would be wrong to tell one by one the things you have bestowed all together, or to split the blessings of a single age by dividing them into words. If I count the wars of my king, I find as many triumphs. No enemy met your onset except to add to your praises. Whoever resisted your will served your trophies, for those who submitted always brought glory to your piety, and those who took up arms against you brought glory to your valour. Whoever saw you in battle was overcome; whoever saw you in peace feared nothing. Your venerable promise did not falter in prosperity, and your vigour suffered no delay in battle. Your path, hemmed in by many obstacles, saw daily victories and brought no loss to your march. It was so blocked by enemy columns that it seemed to deny all passage, and yet so opened by your attack that the enemies' foresight did no harm at all. If these things are to be credited to your good fortune, they are a prince's full dowry; if to your labour, they are more august than any honour. With favourable omens you first took up contests against nature itself, so that your enemies would have no hope left of resisting. You subdued to yourself first the changing laws of the sky, then the defences of the land and the impassable rivers. Call me a liar if heat or cold ever hindered your plans, if you were ever held back by swollen floods or the lack of water, or if the ridges of the Alps, joined to the heights of heaven, ever slowed your course. Those you found once their natural strongholds were overcome did not know how to resist, for broken country makes those it protects feel secure, and those who hold safer ground live with minds slackened by leisure. Against you the dwellers of the plains produced no equals, and those who lived in trackless places saved nothing from plunder once they were in your power, unless they became suppliants. The man who stood without fear displayed his riches, and it did the rebel no good to be known as poor. No one escaped your anger except by humility, since whoever begged was raised to the rank of an ally. The cold of Scythia is not unknown to you, nor are you a stranger to Meroë or to Cancer panting with heat, as if you were lord of another world. By conquering all things you have learned what has barely reached us by hearsay. These things are indeed beyond a man; but whoever is being prepared to steer the world must come trained in all its quarters. Yet I have seized too quickly on the season of your mature praise. As though even a torrent of talent did not run thin at its source, my hunger for the story has made me rush upon the harvest of your full maturity. Whoever tries to set your laurels in order is outrun by their speed and outnumbered by their count. The honours we have recounted, most invincible one, were won by you faster than they can be told. Who would tolerate sluggishness in the telling of his deeds, when he never tolerated it in the doing?

Greece, foreseeing what was to come, raised you in the lap of civilization. When you crossed the threshold of life, she so trained you that the delight she took in you as a boy was soon followed by the security she found in you as a protector. You were still in the white bloom of youth; the milky stalk had not yet yielded its harvest of virtues before being put to the test. Your youthful face was still charming, and no down yet darkened and clothed it. Then the purple of your youth and the bud of the coming empire foreboded terror to those anxious about a change of favour. Then, as if to test your strength and your clemency, madness broke its chains and, feeding on opportunity, took hold of minds made hollow by long peace. At once reverence for the emperor was driven from the city, and a tyrant, called to the throne by no claim of blood, stepped into the vacant possession. Once he held the palace, having beaten his enemies by fear, he decided that nothing remained to be done. Then the light of nature spurred your spirit on before your years could support it, so that the better cause would not go under while you were present, and so that you might repay in a time of need the benefit you had received in peace. At the very first threshold of your attack the usurper gave way, and through you the sceptre was restored to a fugitive who had despaired of his life. Let us sift the histories and question the annals: where is it recorded that a sovereignty won by a man of royal birth with his own blood was handed back to an exile? A camp's glory is shared out among the troops, and what comes from the efforts of many cannot be credited to one man. But the fruit of a unique virtue is restraint of ambition, above all at a time when you could have kept what you had won without loss of reputation. Equal praise is yours, illustrious lord, for the diadem you gave and the diadem you defended. If the ruler of those regions did not love you, he governed the state in fear; if he loved you, he governed it in your debt. You had the purple-clad emperor himself as witness to your merits and your loyalty.

Even then the palace itself had passed into your power, and no one believed that you could not transfer what you had restored to whomever you wished. But you were sparing in claiming rewards, as if they were enough to repay your labours. You accepted the fasces, not so that the curule chair might add lustre to you, but so that the palm-embroidered robe might gain its worth from you. Who would believe that such moderation could live among your familiar qualities alongside the full exercise of valour? That year had a consul who protected the state less by anxious care than by his reputation; when you put on the consular robes, the arms taken up by the enemy trembled. When has fortune ever produced such a one [?] as the proven glory of kings has given us since the infancy of the world? I do not wish to wander through the changing fortunes of dynasties: in your lineage, all who have been found have been proven. The plough brought Serranus to the consular staff; while he committed great seeds to the furrows, a harvest of honours sprang up for him. But I care less for prosperity that begins in desperation. Few have managed to rise nobly above their stock, while you are bound to guard nobly the deeds of your race for your family's sake. Why do you set before me, Antiquity, a peasant's limbs adorned with a general's cloak? I set against you something that surpasses wonder: my prince, born such that he cannot be faulted, and acting as though he were still praying to be counted among emperors.

But what am I to do, faced with so fertile a crop of your deeds, where everything overwhelms the one who must choose? I do not know which ears to bring into the granary and which to leave behind. Before my eyes stands the leader of the Bulgars, struck down by your right hand as it defended freedom. He was not killed, so that he would not be lost as a monument, nor left unharmed, so that he would not live on in arrogance; he would survive among an untamed people as a witness at home to your strength. Had he received a fatal wound, you would have conquered one person; because he remained alive, you subdued his whole race. This is the nation that before you had whatever it wanted. Among them a man won titles by buying rank with the blood of his foes, and the battlefield proclaimed a man's birth, for whoever's weapons were reddened most in the fight was held, beyond dispute, the nobler. Before your battle with them they had never met anyone who resisted, and for long ages they had finished their wars with a single raid. Neither mountain barriers, nor rivers in their path, nor lack of food ever bound them by the narrow law of necessity, since they think it luxury enough to drink mare's milk. Who could withstand an enemy who both rides and feeds by the gift of a swift beast? What of the fact that they impose on these animals too a trained endurance of hunger, and so have learned to escape hunger themselves? How is it that the rider draws food from the vitals of his fasting mount, food which careful training has seen to it that she does not consume? Once they believed the whole world open to them; now they reckon that the only part closed to them is the part you protect. I pass hungrily [?] over much, so that you do not arrive late through the fault of a sluggish pen, and so that the torch of the Roman senate, long forced into shadow, does not shine forth too slowly.

Between your apprenticeship in life and the maturity of your triumphs, heavenly favour poured into your sacred breast a love for us. By then this mighty land had grown old through the cost of long inactivity and the worthlessness of its rulers. Unbroken peace had already exhausted the public wealth, while among us a plunderer from within, swollen by the success of his daily robberies, was himself in want. Prodigal of his own goods, he expected the treasury to grow not so much by taxes as by plunder. A poor master, raging in his ambition, he had earned hatred by his lavishness, and what he stripped from the wealth of those he defrauded won him no goodwill. At that time the narrowness of the court squeezed private fortunes into straits, and the tyrant's fire had died out, letting no sparks from his servants glitter anywhere. He feared his obedient army, which the honour paid to another reminded of its origin; chill with fear, he ordered the legions to march off and return at his nod. Obedience that serves the unworthy is always suspect, and whenever men set over others are conscious of their low birth, they fear the very fact that they are feared. Then a fortunate cause of discord arose between you, when Roman prosperity lured hostile minds to the killing of your kinsmen. The weak provided the cause for fighting, and so that confidence might not come to those doomed to perish [?], a band of fugitives stirred up war. Then, as you summoned your forces far and wide, a single nation scattered among countless peoples was gathered together, a whole world migrating with you to Ausonia. No one set out except in obedience [?]. Wagons were taken in place of houses, and into these moving homes was gathered everything that necessity would require. Then the tools of Ceres and the stones that grind the grain were hauled by oxen. Mothers heavy with child, forgetting their sex and their burden, toiled among your households at the task of preparing food. Then came winter in the open field; the hair was veiled in the constant whiteness of frost, and the beard was matted with icicles. Even the garment a matron had spun with special care to cling to the body cracked in the lasting frost. Food for your columns was supplied either by hostile nations or by wild beasts bred in their lairs.

Among these hardships, which yielded to you whether in ice or in heat, I should like to touch briefly on one episode of your struggle. The river Ulca is the guardian of the Gepids. In place of ramparts it shields that bold people, and like a mountain range it encloses the flank of their province with walls, as it were, that no battering ram could breach. The hard road of your march brought you to this river. There, instead of sending envoys and asking for favour, a nation long unconquered hurried to resist you, at a time when hunger was all but besieging your cohorts before the enemy did. Tell me, I ask you, most clement lord: what hope was left, apart from you, for a people as countless as the sand or the stars? With the Gepids pressing upon you, you flew across a route by a deadly river that even a man in flight would have avoided, straight against swords bared of their sheaths. No one's feet sank and stuck in the mud unawares; no one, careless of life, ran into danger without knowing it. The firmness of the human mind is overcome by seeing danger coming, and the confidence of the brave wavers whenever fearful things are thrust before their eyes. Your unconquered young warriors faced a sure choice among ways of dying, when no hope of safety appeared. Why, ancient records, did you extol Cato for leading an army through the Libyan Syrtes, when he made human deaths the sport of serpents, or when he felt, with no reward for valour, the chill of poison bred by the heat of the sky? No one there saw the water snakes before he saw his death, as his soul, by that monstrous breath, flew off into the air from the frame of the body, as souls are wont to do. A man who does not know where his death comes from does not perish with the praise of the brave. The courage of that soldiery cannot be compared with your troops, nor was its leader's wisdom equal to yours. He was driven by the fury of civil war; you were summoned by Rome, mistress of the world, to restore her state. But why do I put off telling what a favourable outcome brought you? Those whom the far bank had received gave way before the dense ranks of your enemies. Those whom the whirlpool or the charge did not hold were hard pressed by missiles, and lances hurled by stronger arms pierced the starved lattice of their ribs. Then, amid shipwrecks on dry land and waves of blood, the most invincible leader appeared and steadied those around him with these words: 'Whoever wants a way through the enemy line, follow me. Whoever seeks an example of fighting, look to no one else. Valour does not need numbers: wars fall to the few, the fruits of war to the many. The army will be judged by me, and in what I do the nation triumphs. Raise the standards, so that I cannot be hidden; let them know whom they are attacking, and at whose throats they may rest. Let those who meet my charge be ennobled by their death.' With these words he called for a cup as an omen, slackened the reins for battle, and charged headlong. As a torrent lays waste the crops and a lion the herds, so you laid waste, and no one who met you stood firm, nor could anyone escape your pursuit. You were carried through everything, your weapons already failing and your fury still rising. At once the Gepids' situation was reversed, and those who had been scattered were seen, as fortune turned, to be the victors. For you, venerable one, who had seized the first taste of battle alone, now advanced surrounded by thousands. The enemy host was cut down until approaching night snatched a few away. Then your men came upon wagon granaries filled with the stores of cities, which not only met their need but even relieved their fastidiousness amid the abundance of delicacies [?]. So adversity served your prosperity, and the enemy's sally fought against your men's hunger. A clash with the foe overcame starvation, and you would not have regained your strength had there been no battles. Let these few, set in order from among your countless deeds, suffice. I pass over the Sarmatians migrating with their encampment, and I say nothing of the throngs of battles counted among your trophies.

Now I come to you, Odoacer, together with my ruler: you who, like one shaking the world, had roused all nations against him. So many kings had gathered with you for war that the whole people could scarcely have supported so many soldiers. But it was found that the minds of a heaped-up multitude are divided, and that hope of victory does not come from numbers. The right hands of his men were still unsteady from their earlier wasting, and their weak limbs could not carry out the attacks they longed to make. Yet it was enough to be of one will instead of strong, and a single purpose against the enemy brought vengeance in place of strength. Neither a camp long fortified nor the depths of a river held you back; your enemies were allowed to build a rampart, but not to defend it. Suddenly the plains were darkened by fugitives running in all directions, and as they fled across them you charged them with overcoming a storm at home [?]. Meanwhile your battle lines were winning battles by their mere appearance, not by toil. There good fortune opened the doors to you, plainly showing that those who had given way in the first encounter would not face a second struggle. But a wavering mind, deceiving itself, again set up a conflict, preparing a battlefield at your Verona, and the fight was made ready at lavish expense. Before the battle nothing was braver than your adversaries; when the trumpets sounded the signal for war, nothing was weaker. Their valour was greatest in promising combat, and if the tongue could serve for the right hand, their store of words was enormous. They chose a site less suited to fighting than to fear, taking care that the first flight of deserters should not be put down to chance. And yet the bright fortune of the commonwealth urged you on, so that you did not abandon what you had begun. Having covered the stages of your march, you saw the enemy's fires glowing like stars, so that if you had ever known fear you would have learned that you hung over a precipice. But your state of mind was never puffed up by swelling success nor sunk into resignation in times of doubt. The day of battle was at hand, which would bring darkness to many. As soon as Dawn in her saffron chariot announced the rising of the light, and the sun's flame rose from the waters of Ocean, the trumpets were already blaring hoarsely and the army, forgetful of itself, was already looking for you. While you encased your breast in defences of steel, while you put on your greaves, while the sword that avenges liberty was fitted to your side, you comforted your holy mother and venerable sister, who had come to you out of loving care. Their womanly anxiety hung between hope and fear, and as they waited in dread for the outcome they fed their eyes on the star of your face. You strengthened them with these words: 'You know, mother, you whom the honour of your offspring has made known to all nations, that on the day of my birth you bore a man. This is the day on which the battlefield must proclaim your son's manhood. I must act with arms, so that the glories of my ancestors do not perish through me. It is useless to rely on our parents' titles unless our own deeds support us. Before my eyes stands my father, whom fortune never mocked in battle, who won his own successes as his strength demanded. Under this leader I must fight: he did not fear uncertain omens, but made favourable ones for himself. But bring out the finely worked garments, the woven work that tortured the loom; let the battle lines receive me better dressed than festivals are wont to. Let whoever does not know me by my charge recognize me by my splendour. Let the honour of my clothing draw the eyes of the greedy, and let a more precious look show them whom to strike. Let the man to whom you, Fortune, grant my throat have a reward for his labour; let those who never chanced to see me fighting gape at my splendour as I lie fallen.' With these words your charger, restless with longing for the trumpets, took you on its back. But while you lingered over your words, your legions were pressed hard by the enemy's attack. By your delay you gave the sluggish confidence, and I believe this was by the providence of heaven, so that your victory would not be owed to numbers. At once the multitude of the slain announced your arrival to the enemy, and the enormity of the slaughter betrayed who was carrying it out. But they did not lack their usual remedies either. They immediately took the wings that fear provides, choosing destruction in headlong flight for fear of death. Let anyone who thinks I have strayed from the truth look at the waters of the Adige, made rich with corpses by your slaughter: while you swelled its floods with blood, elsewhere the force of its current was dammed. So, lest your swords should not be enough, the water itself fought for you. Hail, most splendid of rivers, who washed away the greater part of Italy's filth, receiving the dregs of the world without loss of your purity! See how that field, once covered with armed men, shines, most glorious with the whiteness of human bones. Whenever we are pressed by the memory of our old grief, we have something to look upon. Let the earth keep this most beautiful scene. Let what they suffered stand on high for as long as oblivion takes to blot out what they did. Oh, if only the ravenous beasts were not allowed to carry anything off! Whatever the thieving beasts have seized is lost from a spectacle we long to see.

I wish, Rome, that you had come there, forgetting your age. Even if you had come trembling on tottering feet, joy would have changed your years. Why do you always shut yourself away, buried in your temples? Here it was brought about that you have more consuls than you once saw candidates. Recognize the clemency of your lord: he wanted you to taste the savour of triumphs, but chose that you should not know the uncertainties of battle.

See how once again that part of the enemy which was owed to death ran to the surrender it already knew. Though those who had fallen were past counting, columns armed with gleaming weapons still gathered to enter your service. Your mind, always inclined to pardon, was moved. You believed that under the schooling of necessity they would grow used to the loyalty they had never shown out of any zeal to win the favour of princes. You were kept safe, foremost of kings, even though you trusted their oath and cast caution aside. We hung in anxiety, afraid that those you had taken in from among your enemies might earn their escape from death. Thanks be to you, God, judge of the world, who drove consciences gripped by long-standing error onto the avenging swords. I would be ashamed to recall your inborn leniency if I did not see that it serves your praise. Why do I hesitate to recount what was done? They chose once more to promise the kingdom to Odoacer, who was holding out an unarmed right hand. At once, when the plot was caught and brought to light, the error of those hostile minds became known. You summoned providence, the companion of your actions. So that the lawlessness of those running about should not go unpunished, you shook the banners of vengeance and secretly made a people already proven sharers in your counsels. No adversary ever learned what the better part of the world was arranging with you. The longed-for slaughter was ordered across the most widely separated regions. Who but the will of heaven brought it about that the plague of the Roman name, gathered over a long age of wickedness, should be poured out at a single stroke of time? Here I do not know where to turn. Shall I give thanks, I who have taken up the office of panegyrist, or shall I go on along the road of your praises that I have begun? The matter was settled by a prosperous and fateful war. Odoacer's presumption was cut down once he found that deceit did him no good. Why should I recall the routed columns of the Heruli? They were led against you so that they might learn here whom they should fear even in their own homes. Another's madness provided the causes of your long quiet. I pass over the lasting peace imposed on you, Burgundian, since you have kept the treaties so faithfully that your living at rest may be credited to constancy, not to fear. And who would let this too fade from memory: that for the good of your fortune we saw the weapons of the faithless clash among themselves, and hostile battle lines fall in a pious encounter while you were busy elsewhere? How often has a man who had vowed to fight against you won victories for you? Let Frederick say, who after breaking faith followed your enemies to their destruction. He brandished his arms against those he had joined in his error, when discord arose among the wicked from the very fact that each knew they wanted one and the same thing. May the Godhead be with us and prolong its blessings forever, for by its ordering the longed-for quarrels arose among the guilty. For Frederick, after he had won you a triumph over your adversaries, furnished from himself [?]…

A great part of your venerable merits draws me to another side. I see an unhoped-for beauty risen from the ashes of cities, and under the fullness of civil order palace roofs gleaming everywhere. I see buildings finished before I had even learned they were planned. Rome herself, the mother of cities, grows young again by cutting away the withered limbs of old age. Forgive me, sacred first beginnings of the Lupercal's guardian spirit: it is a greater thing to defeat decline than to have given a beginning. Add to this that you have veiled the crown of the senate with countless flowers. Despair of office has touched no one who came with a petition and had the goods of a clear conscience to help him. The man who has not asked while poor in splendid merits never has to doubt the outcome of his request. Either we are good by our own resolve or we are shaped by your example. The wealth of the state has grown together with the gains of private persons. Nowhere in your court is there canvassing, and everywhere there is a sharing of wealth. No one goes away without a gift, and no one groans under the hardships of confiscation. Your embassies have an undying vigour. You set out the order of your instructions before you even see the envoys. Nothing is found to contradict your replies, and no easy answer is found to your objections. The prince's foresight keeps watch over the years to come. The care of a great king guards our leisure, and yet you do not stop extending your fortresses, carrying your concerns far into the future. In you neither the brave man's confidence nor the fearful man's caution is lacking. O twofold fullness of virtues in one prince, which reveals God as its author, for among men there is no one from whom it could seem to have taken what it displays!

But see, after a long and solid peace we call our words back to the battle lines. Once more the trumpet summons eloquence. The city of Sirmium was once the frontier of Italy. There the emperors of old kept watch, so that the harm massed by the neighbouring nations should not burst from there into the Roman body. Later, through the neglect of its rulers, it passed under the control of the Gepids, and from there came daily insults and a disorderly stream of embassies. The prince's mind was inflamed by the blandishments of a deceitful schemer and by Thrasaric's ill-timed intimacy with the other Gepids, whose leader is Gunderith. You thought it an injury to you that a possession of Italy should be withheld so long while you ruled. It was not consolation enough that you had not lost it yourself, for your grief was immense that the man who held it had not given it back at the beginning of your reign. You consider an empire that does not grow to be shrinking. When Thrasaric's schemes became plain, you sent the noblest of the Goths, Pitzia and Herduic, with young men not yet consecrated by any battle, so that, if he accepted the terms offered, control of the region might be secured once it was occupied. But the habit of that inconstant man served your good fortune. He fled of his own accord and abandoned what he owed without any push from your army. At once Pitzia, who had learned from you both how to win useful outcomes and how to weigh the moments of decision, believed that the land had not been acquired but restored. He did not plunder it for gain as spoils, but preserved it by good administration as his own. While they were there putting things in order, Greece declared hostility by attacking Mundo, our federate. She brought her Bulgars with her for protection, uses them as a fortress in the clashes of war, and threatens with them. Then Mundo, believing it would be enough for his defence if your troops learned what he was suffering, sent word of his danger by swift messengers. He saw his defenders join battle on his behalf before he learned that they were preparing. When Pitzia caught sight of the untamed Bulgar youth from afar, he armed the burning ardour of his young men with the stronger fire of words: "Remember, comrades, by whose command you have come to these places. Let no one think that the eyes of our king are absent, for it is his fame we must fight for. Even if a shower of spears darkened the sky, the man who hurled his weapon most bravely would not go unseen. Plunge your swords into their breasts, so that from scorn of life may come a clear hope of victory. I suppose the witness who saw our king's strength is now dead, and no one survives who used to tell them what lord we have. Or perhaps they disdain to judge our nation by its prince. Let them understand that what we do flows from him, and let them not be allowed to owe to one person alone what our ruler has passed on to his race." He exchanged these words for the trumpets. At once, as a black storm cloud roars with the rush of gales while the roofs rattle, so the people of Mars plunged headlong into the fray. For a long time the battle wavered in an uncertain balance, as an equal fierceness rose on both sides. Two nations clashed who had never been rescued by flight amid swords. Each marvelled to find the other like itself, and to see that there were people in the human race who would stand against the Goths, or against the Bulgars. Meanwhile, while the fortune of the fight was in doubt and winged deaths claimed the sky, the memory of our prince prevailed, as they strove to make the field bear witness to each man's merits before him. The nation was turned to flight, punished the more heavily because it escaped. The earth was roused and trembled under the pounding of hooves. They hurried away with great lamentation once they saw that their survival was no longer in doubt. God, judge of heaven, multiply the gifts you have bestowed! Those who were never in doubt of triumph, those to whom the whole world looked up, now depart with their war standards lost, struck down by their very survival, crying again and again that those who had fallen were thrice and four times blessed. Why should I recount the slaughter of soldiers and the most shameful withdrawal of the general Sabinianus? It is beyond reason to relate what befell the defenceless man once his protection was destroyed. Then, so that it should not be said [?] that Pitzia, to be celebrated through the ages, fought not so much for glory as for greed, he left the harvest of the field to beasts and birds, for he ordered his hungry soldiers to take nothing from the rich corpses. But what tongues can set these things out adequately? With what gift of eloquence can they be revealed? Long have you conquered in all your encounters. Now you begin to have conquerors in your service. Meanwhile the Roman realms have returned to their old frontier. You lay down laws for the people of Sirmium as the ancients did. Those who until now held what was ours are unsure of their own because you are their neighbour. Why should I speak of the Vandals' raids, which have been checked though the winds obey them [?]? Your friendship is enough for them in place of an annual payment. With wisdom as their guide they do not stray beyond what is permitted. They have earned the right to be neighbours because they do not refuse to obey.

From the heap of your deeds I have set out and recounted these things briefly, with more desire than eloquence, leaving the rest untouched for better speakers. I shall see who surpasses me in eloquence, but no one will be able to surpass me in devotion to you. By God's inspiration you have such gentleness that you believe you can achieve more by love than by fear. Excellent virtues are set among the monuments of your glory, so that while kings fear you, your servants love you. For whatever you command to be given to you, having measured the strength of your subjects, you believe could be refused. O king composed in perfect calm, who credits to our devotion what we pay out of servitude!

What of the fact that you have enclosed the whole Alamannic nation within the borders of Italy without any loss to Roman possessions? It was their lot to have a king after they had deserved to lose one. The nation that always raged in plundering our people has become the guardian of the Latin empire. It turned out happily for them to flee their homeland, for in this way they gained the richness of our soil. You have acquired a land that knows how to yield to the hoe. Although it was not our lot to be spared losses, under you we have seen the best outcomes born from adversity, and the occasion of danger become the mother of prosperity. The one who dwells there, freed from the sedge, rejoices in the land [?], which until now rose above the water only thanks to the firmer rushes, while its dwellings gaped open.

It was fitting too that you should spur eloquence with the rewards of praise, so that we should not let your glories perish in silence. No art lies idle. The skilled man is sought out wherever he hides. The man who deserves office will claim it even if he lives far away. No one whom innocence has made known is ever hidden, since you, a discerning judge, are won not by words but by deeds. The good deeds of our parents who have died are kept in your memory. If a man's loyalty has become known to your clemency, what you owed the father you soon repay to his children by right of inheritance. We enjoy the fruit of our ancestors' services, and yet we do not fear punishment for their faults. Your measured anger ends with the man, while your goodness looks for a successor to reward.

Many things still remain that I could say, but among the many heralds of your deeds it is fitting that something be left untouched. The venerable studies owe it to you that they speak at all. Your predecessors loved ignorance because they never did anything worth praising. The most eloquent man was left to waste away among the ploughs, and what skill had given, force denied. The courts mourned with their advocates silenced, and no prize was granted to the speaker. The outcome of lawsuits tottered at the mercy of chance, since no spirit was given to letters. A single grief had crushed talent everywhere, because idleness was wearing away the powers of the eloquent. Devouring neglect had taken hold of the elders' splendour, and the beginner was not fired by any rivalry worth pursuing. See the riches of your age: then the forums scarcely had accomplished men, and now the church sends forth a panegyrist.

Let antiquity go now and boast of Alexander in its high-buskined tales. The gift of speakers produced a wealth of fame for him, so that with the help of eloquence a beggarly praise seemed to grow in substance. Our king's merits need no advocate to assist them. The deeds of the ancients, though swollen by lies, are smaller than his true acts. You poets feigned great things, but you must confess that our present lord has done greater. The Macedonian leader wanted the sum of his praises to rest on the favour of Choerilus, so that the crowd should not detect his wish to deceive, and so that the man brought in to vouch for his victory should not become a witness to his shamelessness. I take nothing away from the ancients, whom antiquity would have held to be foremost, had not the raising up of the Roman name produced you. Ignorance, the mother of error, held him, for he did not know the true religion. You, a worshipper of the highest God, were formed by life-giving instruction from the very threshold of light. You never credit to your own labours what a favourable outcome has brought. You know that the effort lies with you, but the substance of accomplishment lies with God. You act so as to deserve success, but once you have gained everything you ascribe it to its Author. In strength, vigilance and prosperity you show yourself a prince; in gentleness, a priest. Why did our forebears call those who were given scepters "divine" and "pontiffs" in vain? It is a singular thing to fulfil holiness in deeds and not to bear the venerable names. Let my king be Alamannicus by right, while another bears the name. Let him live as one divine from the fruit of his conscience, and not seek the empty words of pompous boasting, for in his character the flatteries of our forebears serve the truth.

I confess I would like to come down to the end of my speech, overcome by the immensity of your deeds, and pass over your newest glories, dazzled by the light of the earlier ones. Suppose I wished to count the ornaments of the heavenly vault, to take in the brilliance of the Wains and describe the beauty of the sky with a powerless tongue: mortal dimness would give way to divine splendour, and the spark of humble words would not be enough for the lamp of that radiance. In the same way, the very condition that shows me obedient reveals me unequal to the task.

For with what lips should I celebrate this: that you look after the instruments of Gothic strength, taking care that our leisure is not disturbed, and make the untamed youth rehearse war under your eyes amid the blessings of peace? The victorious columns still stand in full strength, and others have already grown up. Arms are hardened by throwing missiles and perform the work of the brave while they play. What in time to come could fully serve valour is now done as a spectacle. While pliant shafts are hurled with boyish throwing-thongs, and bows send their daily deaths to targets ever farther off, the whole precinct of the city is trampled by mock battle. The image of combat is acted out so that real combat may not arise with real danger. Who would believe that one breast could be enough for all this: to conquer in battle with untamed armies, and also to act with such counsel that no cause for fighting arises? We learn that Rutilius and Manlius, with foresight guiding the people, staged gladiatorial combats, so that the common people, held by a long peace, might learn in the theatre seats what happens in the battle line. But then the deaths of comrades were thrust in vain before the eyes of idle hands. Institutions that spring from cruelty are never good. To arm their minds against the enemy, they first watched their own people die. And that contest, as the outcome showed, increased fear more than strength: amid prosperity the minds of the unwarlike learned what to fear. See how far apart these inventions are, separated by the whole width of the road. There the real shedding of blood turned minds away from fighting. Here the vigour of the young is kindled by the image of a feigned contest. Their early youth has taught them to hold in store as many enemy deaths as they have arrows. They are not used to emptying their quivers carelessly in aimless sallies, or hurling certain deaths into the empty air; they mean to take as many lives as the weapons they throw.

But amid the successes of war, with which you train everyone and win favourable omens of victory, you withhold nothing from the sweetness of civil life. Who would believe that your heroes do not reject a fear foreign to them while all is calm? For the law restrains spirits that are untamed in battle. After their laurels they bow their necks to its precepts, and once they have trampled the enemy's wedges, those to whom arms gave way are ruled by decrees. You alone are so formed by merit and by nature that magnanimous men follow your commands. Birth indeed made you a lord, but virtue claimed you as one. The splendour of your race won you the scepter, but even if you lacked its marks, your mind would have caused you to be chosen as prince.

Nor should the beauty of your person be counted among the least of your gifts, since the purple glow of the royal face outshines the purple of rank. Bring out your garments, Seres; offer robes dyed with precious murex that have drunk their nobility from more than one vat. Let a garland be woven of many-coloured gems, and let the stone guarded by the fiercer serpent be brought. Whatever ornaments a compliant world may send will shine the brighter when adorned by the grace of that venerable body. His height reveals the ruler by its stature. The snow of his cheeks is in harmony with their blush. His eyes bloom with unbroken serenity. His hands are worthy to deal death to rebels and the honours they long for to his subjects. Let no one boast of the adornments he puts on, for what diadems do for other lords, nature, with God as craftsman, has done in my king. Wealth and all its aids make those men conspicuous, but a simple and unchanging form has made this man better. Why should those who want borrowed beauty labour over their dress? The ruler of Italy unites two very different things, so that in anger he is like lightning beyond compare, and in joy he is beautiful without a cloud. Even when his lips are still, his countenance promises the envoys of nations either peace when it is gentle or war when it is terrible. You are made up of as many distinctions as would make many men perfect if they were shared out one by one. But may the blessings of a golden age bring forth from you a purple-born offspring! May an heir to the kingdom play in your lap! May a sacred little one demand from us these libations of words that we now offer you, as a testimony to joys like these! See, having paid my debt and done my duty, I have closed my oration with a prayer.
